claim: MAP-C (Mutation Analysis in Pools by Chromosome conformation capture) is a method that simultaneously characterizes the effects of hundreds of cis or trans-acting mutations on a chromosomal contact.
source: Here we describe an assay, MAP-C (Mutation Analysis in Pools by Chromosome conformation capture), that simultaneously characterizes the effects of hundreds of cis or trans-acting mutations on a chromosomal contact.
evidence: The abstract directly states the development and capability of the MAP-C method.

claim: Inducible interchromosomal pairing between HAS1pr-TDA1pr alleles in saturated cultures of Saccharomyces yeast is mediated by three transcription factors: Leu3, Sdd4 (Ypr022c), and Rgt1.
source: Using MAP-C, we show that inducible interchromosomal pairing between HAS1pr-TDA1pr alleles in saturated cultures of Saccharomyces yeast is mediated by three transcription factors, Leu3, Sdd4 (Ypr022c), and Rgt1.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the finding from MAP-C experiments identifying the three transcription factors.

claim: The coincident, combined binding of Leu3, Sdd4, and Rgt1 is strongest at the HAS1pr-TDA1pr locus.
source: The coincident, combined binding of all three factors is strongest at the HAS1pr-TDA1pr locus and is also specific to saturated conditions.
evidence: The abstract states this finding based on the experimental results.

claim: The coincident, combined binding of Leu3, Sdd4, and Rgt1 is specific to saturated conditions.
source: The coincident, combined binding of all three factors is strongest at the HAS1pr-TDA1pr locus and is also specific to saturated conditions.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the condition-specificity of the TF binding.

claim: HAS1pr-TDA1pr pairing requires the structured regulatory domain of Rgt1.
source: We applied MAP-C to further explore the biochemical mechanism of these contacts, and find they require the structured regulatory domain of Rgt1, but no known interaction partners of Rgt1.
evidence: The abstract states this finding from MAP-C experiments.

claim: HAS1pr-TDA1pr pairing does not require known interaction partners of Rgt1.
source: We applied MAP-C to further explore the biochemical mechanism of these contacts, and find they require the structured regulatory domain of Rgt1, but no known interaction partners of Rgt1.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that known interaction partners are not required.

source: In multicellular organisms, active developmental gene promoters form long-range loops with specific enhancer elements (Bonev et al., 2017), and this looping is in some cases sufficient for transcriptional activation (Deng et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Enhancer-promoter looping is in some cases sufficient for transcriptional activation.

evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, genes targeted to nuclear pores are activated.
source: In the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, a well-studied model of genome conformation, genes targeted to nuclear pores are activated (Taddei et al., 2006), while those at the nuclear periphery are repressed (Andrulis et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, genes at the nuclear periphery are repressed.
source: In the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, a well-studied model of genome conformation, genes targeted to nuclear pores are activated (Taddei et al., 2006), while those at the nuclear periphery are repressed (Andrulis et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Motif searches poorly predict TF binding.
source: Although binding site motifs are known for many TFs, motif searches poorly predict TF binding (Guertin and Lis, 2010; Jolma et al., 2015; Le et al., 2018; Levo et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2006; Slattery et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: DNA-bound TFs can recruit other cofactor proteins that can mediate chromosomal contacts.
source: DNA-bound TFs can also recruit other cofactor proteins that can mediate chromosomal contacts (Deng et al., 2012; Monahan et al., 2019; Song et al., 2007), but our understanding of TF-cofactor interactions remains incomplete.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Interchromosomal contacts are less well-understood than intrachromosomal contacts.
source: Among chromosomal contacts and loops, interchromosomal contacts are less well-understood.
evidence: This is a statement of the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The relative paucity of interchromosomal contacts in Hi-C data results from their greater contact distance and chromosomal self-association into territories.
source: This is in part due to the relative paucity of interchromosomal contacts in Hi-C and other 3C (chromosome conformation capture) data, which results from their greater contact distance (Maass et al., 2018) and chromosomal self-association into territories (Cremer and Cremer, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Known classes of interchromosomal contacts include clustering of transcriptionally active genes.
source: Nevertheless, many distinct classes of interchromosomal contacts are known, including clustering of transcriptionally active genes (Mitchell and Fraser, 2008; Osborne et al., 2004; Schoenfelder et al., 2010), associations with nuclear bodies (Quinodoz et al., 2018), interactions among developmental enhancers and promoters (Lomvardas et al., 2006; Monahan et al., 2019), and mitotic homologous chromosome pairing in organisms ranging from yeast (Burgess et al., 1999) to flies (Henikoff and Dreesen, 1989; Joyce et al., 2016; Morris et al., 1999) and mammals (Xu et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Known classes of interchromosomal contacts include associations with nuclear bodies.

claim: Loop extrusion by cohesin and other SMC factors is thought to primarily mediate intrachromosomal loops.
source: The emerging consensus model for such DNA-DNA interactions involves loop extrusion by cohesin and other Structural Maintenance of Chromosomes (SMC) factors, which is thought to primarily mediate intrachromosomal loops (Alipour and Marko, 2012; Rao et al., 2014; Rowley and Corces, 2018; Sanborn et al., 2015; Swygert et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: SMC complexes are capable of mediating interactions between multiple DNA molecules, such as between sister chromatids.
source: However, SMC complexes are also capable of mediating interactions between multiple DNA molecules, such as between sister chromatids (Michaelis et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Interchromosomal contacts can be mediated by dimerization of structured proteins.
source: Interchromosomal contacts (Monahan et al., 2019) and intrachromosomal contacts (Weintraub et al., 2017; Deng et al., 2012) can also be mediated by dimerization of structured proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Intrachromosomal contacts can be mediated by dimerization of structured proteins.
source: Interchromosomal contacts (Monahan et al., 2019) and intrachromosomal contacts (Weintraub et al., 2017; Deng et al., 2012) can also be mediated by dimerization of structured proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Weak interactions such as phase separation of nuclear factors may play an important role in shaping 3D genome organization.
source: In addition to these well-defined strong molecular interactions, weak interactions such as those underlying phase separation of nuclear factors such as transcription factors (Boija et al., 2018; Chong et al., 2018), coactivators (Cho et al., 2018), RNA polymerase (Boehning et al., 2018), and heterochromatin proteins (Larson et al., 2017; Strom et al., 2017) may play an important role in shaping 3D genome organization.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mitotic homologous chromosome pairing occurs along the length of the genome in Drosophila.
source: Homolog pairing occurs along the length of the genome in Drosophila (Joyce et al., 2016), but is more subtle in yeast and other organisms, where the association is often transient and/or genomically localized (Xu et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Homolog pairing is more subtle in yeast and other organisms, where the association is often transient and/or genomically localized.
source: Homolog pairing occurs along the length of the genome in Drosophila (Joyce et al., 2016), but is more subtle in yeast and other organisms, where the association is often transient and/or genomically localized (Xu et al., 2006).

claim: In mammals, X chromosome pairing is mediated by CTCF and Oct4.
source: In mammals, X chromosome pairing is mediated by CTCF and Oct4 (Donohoe et al., 2009), in conjunction with transcription (Xu et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: X chromosome pairing in mammals occurs in conjunction with transcription.
source: In mammals, X chromosome pairing is mediated by CTCF and Oct4 (Donohoe et al., 2009), in conjunction with transcription (Xu et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: A novel example of an inducible, localized interchromosomal contact between homologous copies of the HAS1pr-TDA1pr locus in diploid Saccharomyces yeasts was recently identified.
source: We recently identified a novel example of an inducible, localized interchromosomal contact between homologous copies of the HAS1pr-TDA1pr locus in diploid Saccharomyces yeasts (Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: HAS1pr-TDA1pr interchromosomal contact occurs in saturated culture conditions.
source: This interaction occurs in saturated culture conditions, requires the 1 kb intergenic region between the HAS1 and TDA1 coding sequences, and is detectable by both Hi-C and microscopy.
evidence: This claim is stated based on prior research by the authors.

claim: HAS1pr-TDA1pr interchromosomal contact requires the 1 kb intergenic region between the HAS1 and TDA1 coding sequences.
source: This interaction occurs in saturated culture conditions, requires the 1 kb intergenic region between the HAS1 and TDA1 coding sequences, and is detectable by both Hi-C and microscopy.
evidence: This claim is stated based on prior research by the authors.

claim: HAS1pr-TDA1pr interchromosomal contact is detectable by both Hi-C and microscopy.
source: This interaction occurs in saturated culture conditions, requires the 1 kb intergenic region between the HAS1 and TDA1 coding sequences, and is detectable by both Hi-C and microscopy.
evidence: This claim is stated based on prior research by the authors.

claim: Yeast TF binding is well-characterized for standard growth conditions.
source: Although yeast TF binding is well-characterized for standard growth conditions (Badis et al., 2008), TF binding has not been systematically measured in saturated culture conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: TF binding has not been systematically measured in saturated culture conditions.
source: Although yeast TF binding is well-characterized for standard growth conditions (Badis et al., 2008), TF binding has not been systematically measured in saturated culture conditions.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field at the time of the study.

claim: A ~150 bp region is sufficient for HAS1pr-TDA1pr interchromosomal pairing.
source: Compared to the genomic libraries, the 3C libraries were highly enriched for a narrow region spanning ~ 500 to ~ 700 bp from the HAS1 coding sequence, with a plateau between ~ 525 to ~ 675 bp, consistent with that ~ 150 bp region being the only subsequence shorter than 178 bp sufficient for pairing (termed the 'minimal pairing region' below).
evidence: This claim is based on the cis MAP-C experimental results showing enrichment of specific subsequences.

claim: Insertion of the minimal pairing region into an ectopic location induces pairing with the native HAS1pr-TDA1pr locus in saturated cultures of haploid S. cerevisiae.
source: Indeed, insertion of the minimal pairing region led to a > 30 fold increase in 3C signal for pairing with HAS1pr-TDA1pr as compared to the negative control (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Six clusters of two or more adjacent positions in the minimal pairing region show strong depletion of substitutions in the 3C libraries, indicating they are required for HAS1pr-TDA1pr pairing.
source: This identified six clusters of two or more adjacent positions showing strong depletion of substitutions in the 3C libraries, indicating that they are required for HAS1pr-TDA1pr pairing (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is based on error-prone PCR cis MAP-C experimental results shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The first two clusters of positions required for pairing align to a Leu3 motif.
source: The first two clusters together aligned to a Leu3 motif (Figure 1E), the third to several similar motifs, including Sdd4 (Ypr022c) and Mig1 (Figure 1F), and the last three to Rgt1 motifs in both orientations (Figure 1G–I).
evidence: This claim is based on motif analysis of the cis MAP-C results shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The third cluster of positions required for pairing aligns to Sdd4 and Mig1 motifs.
source: The first two clusters together aligned to a Leu3 motif (Figure 1E), the third to several similar motifs, including Sdd4 (Ypr022c) and Mig1 (Figure 1F), and the last three to Rgt1 motifs in both orientations (Figure 1G–I).
evidence: This claim is based on motif analysis of the cis MAP-C results shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The last three clusters of positions required for pairing align to Rgt1 motifs in both orientations.
source: The first two clusters together aligned to a Leu3 motif (Figure 1E), the third to several similar motifs, including Sdd4 (Ypr022c) and Mig1 (Figure 1F), and the last three to Rgt1 motifs in both orientations (Figure 1G–I).
evidence: This claim is based on motif analysis of the cis MAP-C results shown in Figures 1G-I.

claim: Deletion of RGT1 led to a ~20 fold decrease in pairing strength in the pilot trans MAP-C screen.
source: However, deletion of RGT1 led to a ~ 20 fold decrease in pairing strength, consistent with Rgt1 binding its cognate motifs in the minimal pairing region (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This claim is based on trans MAP-C experimental results shown in Figures 2B and C.

claim: LEU3 and RGT1 knockouts were depleted ~4 fold from the 3C libraries in the full trans MAP-C screen.
source: However, LEU3 and RGT1 knockouts were depleted ~ 4 fold from the 3C libraries, suggesting that they are required for pairing (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is based on trans MAP-C experimental results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Deletion of MOT3 modestly decreased pairing (~2.5 fold).
source: In addition, deletion of MOT3 modestly decreased pairing (~2.5 fold); however, its binding motif is not present in the HAS1pr-TDA1pr region, suggesting an indirect role.
evidence: This claim is based on trans MAP-C experimental results.

claim: SDD4 is required for HAS1pr-TDA1pr pairing.
source: We found that SDD4 is indeed required for pairing, suggesting that it is the trans-acting factor that binds the CCCCAC motif (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is based on trans MAP-C experimental results shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Leu3, Sdd4, and Rgt1 strongly bind to the HAS1pr-TDA1pr pairing region in saturated conditions.
source: By qPCR using two different primer pairs, all three TFs strongly bound to the HAS1pr-TDA1pr pairing region in saturated conditions, but near background levels in exponential growth (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This claim is based on ChIP-qPCR experimental results shown in Figures 2D and E.

claim: Leu3, Sdd4, and Rgt1 bind to the HAS1pr-TDA1pr pairing region at near background levels in exponential growth.
source: By qPCR using two different primer pairs, all three TFs strongly bound to the HAS1pr-TDA1pr pairing region in saturated conditions, but near background levels in exponential growth (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This claim is based on ChIP-qPCR experimental results shown in Figures 2D and E.

claim: All three TFs (Leu3, Sdd4, and Rgt1) show robust ChIP-seq peaks at HAS1pr-TDA1pr in saturated conditions.
source: Consistent with our quantitative PCR measurements, all three TFs showed robust ChIP-seq peaks at HAS1pr-TDA1pr in saturated conditions.
evidence: This claim is based on ChIP-seq experimental results.

claim: Only Leu3 demonstrates a significant ChIP-seq peak at HAS1pr-TDA1pr in exponential growth, with 20-fold weaker enrichment compared to saturated conditions.
source: In contrast, only Leu3 demonstrated a significant peak in exponential growth, with 20-fold weaker enrichment (2.5-fold vs. 51-fold in saturated conditions; Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is based on ChIP-seq experimental results shown in Figure 2F.

claim: TDA1pr exhibits the strongest total ChIP-seq signal in saturated conditions among loci with motif clusters containing all three TF motifs in both S. cerevisiae and S. uvarum.
source: Of these six loci, TDA1pr exhibited the strongest total ChIP-seq signal in saturated conditions (Figure 3B and C), even when extending the search to motif clusters with only one or two of the three motifs in S. cerevisiae (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figures 3B and C.

claim: HXT3pr exhibits inducible homolog pairing in saturated culture conditions.
source: We observed that HXT3pr appears to form inducible homologous contacts in saturated culture conditions (Figure 3D), despite weak Sdd4 and no Leu3 binding.
evidence: This claim is based on Hi-C experimental results shown in Figure 3D.

claim: HXT3 promoters exhibit 1.6- to 2.7-fold increased interaction frequencies compared to other similar interchromosomal pairs of loci in saturated culture conditions across several strain backgrounds.
source: Across several strain backgrounds, the HXT3 promoters exhibited 1.6- to 2.7-fold increased interaction frequencies compared to other similar interchromosomal pairs of loci (at least 480 kb from a centromere and excluding subtelomeric regions) in saturated culture conditions (Figure 3E), but only at baseline levels during exponential growth in rich medium.
evidence: This claim is based on Hi-C experimental results shown in Figure 3E.

claim: HXT3 promoters exhibit only baseline interaction frequencies during exponential growth in rich medium.
source: Across several strain backgrounds, the HXT3 promoters exhibited 1.6- to 2.7-fold increased interaction frequencies compared to other similar interchromosomal pairs of loci (at least 480 kb from a centromere and excluding subtelomeric regions) in saturated culture conditions (Figure 3E), but only at baseline levels during exponential growth in rich medium.
evidence: This claim is based on Hi-C experimental results shown in Figure 3E.

claim: In all saturated culture datasets where homolog pairing was present, inter-locus interactions between HAS1pr-TDA1pr and HXT3pr were substantially weaker and similar in frequency to those in non-pairing conditions.
source: In all saturated culture datasets where homolog pairing was present, inter-locus interactions were substantially weaker and similar in frequency to those in non-pairing conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on Hi-C experimental results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Interchromosomal pairing mediated by Leu3, Sdd4, and Rgt1 is sequence-specific beyond the simple presence of the same TF binding sites.
source: Together with our previous experiment demonstrating that two identical copies of the minimal pairing region can pair even at non-allelic locations in haploid S. cerevisiae (Figure 1C), these data suggest that the interchromosomal pairing mediated by Leu3, Sdd4, and Rgt1 is sequence-specific beyond the simple presence of the same TF binding sites.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combination of experimental results showing pairing at identical sequences but not between different loci with the same TF binding sites.

claim: RGT1 is upregulated ~2 fold in saturated cultures compared to exponentially growing cultures.
source: RGT1 and SDD4 were upregulated in saturated cultures, ~ 2 fold and ~ 6 fold, respectively, whereas LEU3 transcript levels remained constant (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is based on RNA-seq experimental results shown in Figure 4A.

claim: SDD4 is upregulated ~6 fold in saturated cultures compared to exponentially growing cultures.
source: RGT1 and SDD4 were upregulated in saturated cultures, ~ 2 fold and ~ 6 fold, respectively, whereas LEU3 transcript levels remained constant (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is based on RNA-seq experimental results shown in Figure 4A.

claim: LEU3 transcript levels remain constant between saturated and exponentially growing cultures.
source: RGT1 and SDD4 were upregulated in saturated cultures, ~ 2 fold and ~ 6 fold, respectively, whereas LEU3 transcript levels remained constant (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is based on RNA-seq experimental results shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Individual overexpression of Leu3, Sdd4, or Rgt1 is not sufficient to produce pairing in non-saturated culture conditions.
source: In all three strains, a 2 hr estradiol induction led to no increase in pairing strength despite between 2- and 10-fold increases in transcript levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is based on estradiol induction experiments and 3C measurements shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Deletion of TUP1 or SSN6 both led to increased pairing.
source: Deletion of TUP1 or SSN6 both led to increased pairing, indicating that the recruitment of the Tup1/Ssn6 co-repressor complex inhibits pairing.
evidence: This claim is based on trans MAP-C experimental results shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Recruitment of the Tup1/Ssn6 co-repressor complex inhibits pairing.
source: Deletion of TUP1 or SSN6 both led to increased pairing, indicating that the recruitment of the Tup1/Ssn6 co-repressor complex inhibits pairing.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that deletion of TUP1 or SSN6 increases pairing.

claim: Deletion of MTH1 or STD1 had a minimal negative effect on pairing.
source: Deletion of MTH1 or STD1 had a minimal negative effect on pairing.
evidence: This claim is based on trans MAP-C experimental results shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Much of the C-terminal half of Rgt1 is required for HAS1pr-TDA1pr pairing.
source: Surprisingly, much of the C-terminal half of Rgt1 was required for HAS1pr-TDA1pr pairing.
evidence: This claim is based on trans MAP-C experimental results with Rgt1 deletion mutants shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The regions of Rgt1 required for pairing are closely aligned to the regions predicted to be highly structured, largely through alpha helices.
source: These 'pairing domains' are closely aligned to the regions of Rgt1 predicted to be highly structured, largely through alpha helices (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of trans MAP-C results with protein structure predictions shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Deletion of the zinc finger DNA-binding domain of Rgt1 led to background pairing levels, equivalent to lacking Rgt1 altogether.
source: As expected, deletion of the zinc finger DNA-binding domain or the C-terminal domain led to background pairing levels, equivalent to lacking Rgt1 altogether.
evidence: This claim is based on trans MAP-C experimental results with Rgt1 domain deletion mutants shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Deletion of the C-terminal domain of Rgt1 led to background pairing levels, equivalent to lacking Rgt1 altogether.
source: As expected, deletion of the zinc finger DNA-binding domain or the C-terminal domain led to background pairing levels, equivalent to lacking Rgt1 altogether.
evidence: This claim is based on trans MAP-C experimental results with Rgt1 domain deletion mutants shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Deletion of the Q/N-rich domain of Rgt1 led to stronger pairing than the wild-type control.
source: Surprisingly, deletion of the Q/N-rich domain led to stronger pairing than the wild-type control (with RGT1 integrated at the same ectopic location), suggesting that the Q/N-rich domain inhibits pairing.
evidence: This claim is based on trans MAP-C experimental results with Rgt1 domain deletion mutants shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The Q/N-rich domain of Rgt1 inhibits pairing.
source: Surprisingly, deletion of the Q/N-rich domain led to stronger pairing than the wild-type control (with RGT1 integrated at the same ectopic location), suggesting that the Q/N-rich domain inhibits pairing.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that deletion of the Q/N-rich domain increases pairing.

claim: Both the S88A and S758A mutations in Rgt1 had a weak decrease in pairing.
source: Both the S88A and S758A mutations had a weak decrease in pairing, indicating that although these mutations are capable of disrupting Rgt1 activator function and intramolecular interactions (Polish et al., 2005), they do not individually play major roles in regulation of pairing in saturated cultures.
evidence: This claim is based on trans MAP-C experimental results with Rgt1 phosphorylation site mutants shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Rgt1 binding site mutations led to higher levels of S. cerevisiae TDA1 in saturated culture conditions.
source: The Rgt1 binding site mutations led to higher levels of S. cerevisiae TDA1, consistent with Rgt1 acting as a repressor under low glucose conditions (Figure 5B), but had no significant effect on either S. uvarum HAS1 or TDA1.
evidence: This claim is based on RNA-seq experimental results shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Rgt1 acts as a repressor of TDA1 under low glucose conditions.
source: The Rgt1 binding site mutations led to higher levels of S. cerevisiae TDA1, consistent with Rgt1 acting as a repressor under low glucose conditions (Figure 5B), but had no significant effect on either S. uvarum HAS1 or TDA1.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Rgt1 binding site mutations increase TDA1 expression.

claim: Rgt1 binding site mutations had no significant effect on S. uvarum HAS1 or TDA1 expression.

evidence: This claim is based on RNA-seq experimental results shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Disrupting the Leu3 binding site had no significant effect on HAS1 or TDA1 transcript levels.
source: Surprisingly, despite the conserved binding site and strong ChIP-seq signal for Leu3 in HAS1pr-TDA1pr, disrupting its binding site had no significant effect on the transcript levels of any gene (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is based on RNA-seq experimental results shown in Figure 5C.

claim: None of the TF deletion strains (leu3Δ, sdd4Δ, rgt1Δ) had altered HAS1 expression in saturated culture conditions.
source: Focusing on the HAS1-TDA1 locus, none of the deletion strains had altered HAS1 expression, and only the rgt1∆ strain had even slightly altered TDA1 expression (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is based on RNA-seq experimental results shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Only the rgt1Δ strain had slightly altered TDA1 expression in saturated culture conditions.
source: Focusing on the HAS1-TDA1 locus, none of the deletion strains had altered HAS1 expression, and only the rgt1∆ strain had even slightly altered TDA1 expression (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is based on RNA-seq experimental results shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Leu3, Sdd4, and Rgt1 do not play a major role in transcriptional regulation of HAS1 or TDA1 in saturated culture conditions as detected by standard polyA mRNA sequencing.
source: These results are consistent with our earlier results from mutating TF binding sites, and together indicate that despite the importance of Leu3, Sdd4, and Rgt1 binding for pairing at the HAS1pr-TDA1pr locus in saturated culture conditions, they do not play a major role in transcriptional regulation as detected by standard polyA mRNA sequencing.
evidence: This claim is based on RNA-seq experimental results from both binding site mutations and TF deletions.
